explanations.explanation: Footing is it. David says he has sunk into the miry depths, where there is no footing. That's mud with nothing solid under it, and no way to push off. I know that feeling, friend, because I once lost a whole afternoon stuck in a dough bowl.

Deep water does sound dark, so I see why you went there. But David doesn't say the light is missing. He says there's no footing, which means nothing solid under his feet. He's sunk into the miry depths, and the trouble is that he can't stand up.

Shelter makes sense when you think of trouble, but that's not the word David uses. He's sunk in the mud and drifting in deep water, where the flood engulfs him. What he says is missing is footing, something firm to stand on.
Not quite, baker. David says the opposite. He calls them those who hate him "without cause" and says they are his enemies "for no reason." So the text says his haters have no good reason at all.
Right, and David says it twice. They hate him "without cause," and they are his enemies "for no reason." Trouble like that is hard enough when you've earned it. It's worse when you haven't.
Repay is the word. David says, "Though I did not steal, I must repay." He's making good on something he didn't take. That is not a fun bill to open.
Running away would be a natural move, but that's not what David says. He says that even though he did not steal, he must repay. He's the one paying up for something he didn't take.
With that many enemies, fighting is a fair guess. But David's line is about something else. He says he did not steal, yet he must repay. It's a debt on his shoulders, not a battle.

explanations.answer: That they not be ashamed through him
explanations.explanation: Yes. David says, "May those who hope in You not be ashamed through me…" He just admitted his folly, and now he's thinking about the people who hope in God. I think that's a man who knows his life touches other people.

explanations.answer: That they come and rescue him
explanations.explanation: Close, because David is asking for rescue all over this psalm. But he asks God for it, not the people who hope in God. In verse 6 his request is that they not be ashamed through him. He's thinking about how his life affects them.

I get the thought, since David is carrying a lot of shame. But he doesn't ask for anyone to forget him. He prays, "May those who hope in You not be ashamed through me…" His worry is how they'll be affected.

That's the one. David says, "…zeal for Your house has consumed me…" His love for God's house burns so hot that it costs him, and he becomes a stranger to his own brothers. That's a lot to carry for loving the right thing.
A falling out with family does sound like anger. But David names a different cause. He says it's because zeal for God's house has consumed him. He gives no reason for any anger at his brothers.
He has plenty of enemies, so fear would make sense. But when David explains why he's a stranger to his brothers, he says, "…zeal for Your house has consumed me…" That's what's burning in him.

Yes. David says, "…the insults of those who insult You have fallen on me." The people insulting God are throwing it at David. When you stand close to something you love, you can catch what's thrown at it.
Look again, friend, because David does say it. In verse 9 he says, "…the insults of those who insult You have fallen on me." The insults aimed at God land on him.

That's how we'd hope it goes, but the text says otherwise. David says, "I wept and fasted, but it brought me reproach." He also says he was sport to them when he wore sackcloth. People made fun of him.
Right. David says, "I wept and fasted, but it brought me reproach." And when he made sackcloth his clothing, he says he was "sport to them." He opens his heart and they treat it like a joke.
Yes. Right after the mocking, David says, "But my prayer to You, O LORD, is for a time of favor." Look at that little word "But." The song of the drunkards doesn't get the last word.
Plenty of us would be tempted, but David doesn't. After the mocking, he says, "But my prayer to You, O LORD, is for a time of favor." He turns toward God, not toward a comeback.
Walking out of town is a fair thought after that. But the psalm doesn't say he leaves. What he says comes next is, "But my prayer to You, O LORD, is for a time of favor." He prays.
That's it. David prays, "In Your abundant loving devotion, O God, answer me with Your sure salvation." He's leaning on who God is. In verse 16 he says it again: "Your loving devotion is good."
David doesn't bring a spotless record, friend. In verse 5 he says, "You know my folly, O God." What he leans on is God's abundant loving devotion.
Hold on, David says his brothers see him as a stranger (v.8). So he isn't counting on them. He asks God to answer him "In Your abundant loving devotion." That's where his hope sits.
I can see why you'd think so, but David says the opposite. In verse 17 he says, "Answer me quickly!" That's a man in distress asking for an answer fast.
Right. David is in distress, and he says, "Answer me quickly!" He doesn't pretend to be calm about it. He tells God plainly that he needs help soon.
Yes. David asks, "Draw near to my soul and redeem me…" He wants God close, not far off. I think when you're stuck in the deep, close is the whole point.
Rest sounds nice, but David isn't asking for God to leave him alone. He's asking for the opposite. He says, "Draw near to my soul and redeem me…"
David is already in the middle of trouble, so he isn't asking for a test. He asks God to draw near to his soul and redeem him. He's asking for rescue, not another trial.

That's right. David says, "I looked for sympathy, but there was none, for comforters, but I found no one." He looked around and nobody was there. I think that's one of the loneliest lines in the psalm.
That would be nice, but David doesn't say that. Earlier he says he's a stranger to his brothers (v.8). When he looks for comforters, he says he finds no one.
I'd love for the psalm to say that, friend. But David says, "…for comforters, but I found no one." He doesn't find a friend there. He finds no one, so the only one left to turn to is God.

explanations.answer: They persecute the one God struck
explanations.explanation: Yes. David says, "For they persecute the one You struck and recount the pain of those You wounded." His reason is how they treat people who are already hurting. This is a heavy part of the psalm.

explanations.answer: They mock the ones God healed
explanations.explanation: I see the idea, but David says it differently. His words are about those God struck and wounded, not healed. He says they "recount the pain of those You wounded." It's a heavy verse.

explanations.answer: They scorn the ones God blessed
explanations.explanation: That's not the reason David gives. In verse 26 he says they persecute the one God struck. He also says they recount the pain of those God wounded. It's a heavy part of the psalm, and I think it hurts to read.

Yes. Right after those hard words, David says, "But I am in pain and distress; let Your salvation protect me, O God." He goes right back to being honest with God about where he hurts. And he asks for salvation.
I understand why it might seem that way, but David does say it. In verse 29 he says, "But I am in pain and distress; let Your salvation protect me, O God." The text puts his pain right there.

That's it. David says his praise "will please the LORD more than an ox, more than a bull with horns and hooves." A song of thanks from a man who was just up to his neck in water. I think that tells you a lot about what he treasures.
Silver would be a fair guess, but David never says it. He says his praise will please the LORD "more than an ox, more than a bull with horns and hooves." That's the comparison he picks.
A golden altar sounds fancy, but David doesn't mention one. He says his praise will please the LORD "more than an ox, more than a bull with horns and hooves." That's the thing he says it beats.
David says the opposite. In verse 33 he says, "For the LORD listens to the needy and does not despise His captive people." The LORD listens to them.
Right. David says the LORD "listens to the needy and does not despise His captive people." That is good news for anyone who has felt forgotten.
Rebuild is right. David says, "For God will save Zion and rebuild the cities of Judah…" Zion is a name for Jerusalem. The psalm that started in the mud ends with rebuilding.
Scattering is the opposite direction, friend. David says God will save Zion and rebuild the cities of Judah. That part of the psalm is about putting things back.
I get why you'd think so, since David has gone through some hard stretches. But verse 35 says God will save Zion and rebuild the cities of Judah. The word is rebuild.
That's right. David says, "…those who love His name will settle in it." It's not about strength or riches. It's about love for God's name.
Warriors would be a natural guess for cities, but that's not what David says. Verse 36 says the descendants of His servants will inherit it. Then it says those who love His name will settle in it.
Money would make sense for a city, friend, but David doesn't say that. He says, "…those who love His name will settle in it." What counts there is love for God's name, not a bank balance.
